html:
The Dutch East India Company ran a large slave trade across the Indian Ocean and the Indonesian islands from the 1620s until it was dissolved in 1799. Historians estimate that between about 660,000 and 1.1 million enslaved people passed through its ports and territories.

Slavery existed in the islands before the Dutch came, but the company's towns depended on it. Captives came from India and Bengal, from Bali and Sulawesi, from Arakan in Burma and from Madagascar. Enslaved people made up a large part of the population of Batavia, working as servants, craftsmen and labourers. After the Dutch conquest of Banda, enslaved workers ran the nutmeg plantations there. The company also shipped enslaved Asians and Africans to the Cape Colony.

This trade is less well known than the Atlantic slave trade, partly because it was spread over many small routes. The Netherlands abolished slavery in the Dutch East Indies in 1860.
